deep.reconstruction:
This page closes Euler's practical consequences (§§XLIV–XLVI) of his buckling theory for columns. Earlier sections established that the load at which a column begins to bend is P = π²·Ekk/a², where Ekk is the bending stiffness. He also showed that self-weight lowers this only slightly, and that for one material the stiffness varies as the fourth power of the diameter.

(1) Cylinder. Calibrate on a small model with height a, diameter d and load p. A cylinder of height A and diameter D then carries P = (a²D⁴/(A²d⁴))·p.

(2) Truncated cone. With end diameters D and E, Euler gives P = (a²D²E²/(A²d⁴))·p. In modern terms, the stiffness is K u⁴ with u = f + gx linear in x. The equation K u⁴ y'' + P y = 0 has the exact solution y = u·sin(√(P/K)/(g u) + φ). Requiring y = 0 at both ends gives √(P/K)(1/u₁ − 1/u₂)/g = π. Hence P = π² K u₁² u₂²/A². So the formula is exact for a pin-ended conical column, not an approximation. The effective stiffness is the geometric mean √(I₁I₂) of the end stiffnesses.

(3) Other materials need their own model. This amounts to calibrating E experimentally.

(4) §XLV, square–cube argument for buckling. Geometrically similar columns scaled by n carry n² times the load. Their own weight, and the weight of similar buildings they support, grows as n³. So architects' practice of keeping proportions fixed (the orders) makes tall columns relatively weaker.

(5) §XLVI. To carry n³p at height na, set D⁴/(na)² = n³d⁴/a². This gives D⁴ = n⁵d⁴, so D = n·d·n^{1/4}. The table on the next page follows, and §XLVII generalises it to D = d(m n²)^{1/4}: diameter ∝ height^{1/2}·load^{1/4}.
errors: None on this page; the formulas P ∝ D⁴/A², P ∝ D²E²/A² (exact for a pin-ended cone) and D = n^{5/4}d are correct.

The table on the following page has two wrong entries. For 3a it should be 3^{5/4} = 3.9482, not 3.9528. For 10a it should be 10^{5/4} = 17.7828, not 17.3828; the second may be a misprint or a transcription error. Also 4^{5/4} = 5.65685, which Euler truncates to 5.6568.

ideas.what: Scaling of the critical buckling load with diameter and height, calibrated from a small model
ideas.modern_name: Euler buckling load P ∝ EI/L², I ∝ D⁴; model testing
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1744 Methodus inveniendi, Additamentum I; 1757 E238)

ideas.what: Critical load of a truncated-cone column equals π²K(D E)²/A², i.e. effective stiffness is the geometric mean of the end stiffnesses
ideas.modern_name: Exact buckling load of a tapered column with I ∝ (linear)⁴ (Dinnik-type solution)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Often cited in engineering texts via Dinnik (early 20th c.); Euler's priority is discussed by Truesdell (1960)

ideas.what: Square–cube argument applied to elastic stability: similar columns carry loads ∝ n² while the weights to be carried grow as n³
ideas.usually_credited_to: Galileo (Discorsi 1638) for fracture; here extended to buckling by Euler

ideas.what: Design rule: diameter ∝ height^{1/2}·load^{1/4}; for load ∝ height³, diameter ∝ height^{5/4}
ideas.modern_name: Stability-based allometric design rule (cf. later Greenhill-type tree-height and column-proportion scaling)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler 1757; analogous allometric arguments later by Greenhill (1881) and McMahon (1973) for trees

missed.claim: Euler's buckling-based scaling D ∝ L^{1/2}P^{1/4}, with D ∝ L^{5/4} for similar superstructures, anticipates the elastic-stability allometry used in biology. Examples are Greenhill's maximal tree height and McMahon's elastic-similarity rule D ∝ L^{3/2}. Euler's earlier priority for stability-driven (rather than strength-driven) scaling is rarely cited in that literature.
missed.quote: leur épaisseur doit être augmentée dans une plus grande raison que leur hauteur, & on ne sauroit plus les former sur le même modele
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is an attribution and historical note for allometry and structural-scaling literature; it is not new mathematics.

deep.surprise_reason: The scaling consequences are routine, and E238 is well covered by Truesdell. The cone formula is exact and somewhat under-credited in engineering texts, but it is known.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image; no substantive corrections needed (the formula reads P = aaDDEE·p/(AAd⁴), and the diameter rule reads nd·⁴√n).
